formulas.title: Speed
formulas.explanation: In uniform rectilinear motion (URM), the body moves in a straight line with constant speed. The average speed is equal to the instantaneous speed and is calculated as the ratio of the distance traveled (d) to the time interval (t). SI unit of measurement: m/s. Example: a car that travels 120 km in 2 hours has a speed of v = 120/2 = 60 km/h.

formulas.title: Speed
formulas.explanation: The velocity at a given instant in MRUV depends on the initial velocity (v₀), constant acceleration (a) and time (t). If a > 0, the body accelerates; if a < 0, the body brakes. This equation follows from the definition of acceleration: a = Δv/Δt. Example: a body launched with v₀ = 5 m/s and a = 2 m/s² has after 3 s the speed v = 5 + 2·3 = 11 m/s.

formulas.title: Distance
formulas.explanation: Space law in MRUV: position (or distance traveled) depends on initial velocity, time and acceleration. The term v₀·t corresponds to the uniform motion, and ½·a·t² is the acceleration contribution. The graph of x(t) is a parabola. In free fall (v₀ = 0, a = g): x = ½·g·t².

formulas.title: Torricelli
formulas.explanation: Torricelli's equation relates final velocity to initial velocity, acceleration, and distance traveled without explicitly depending on time. Useful when the time is unknown. It is obtained by eliminating t from the equations v = v₀ + at and x = v₀t + ½at². In free fall: v² = 2gh.

formulas.title: Acceleration
formulas.explanation: Average acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time. In MRUV, acceleration is constant. SI unit: m/s². Gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface: g ≈ 9.8 m/s². Sign: a > 0 (acceleration), a < 0 (deceleration/braking).

formulas.title: Law I
formulas.formula: \( \Sigma F = 0 \) — corp în repaus sau mișcare uniformă
formulas.explanation: Law of Inertia: A body remains at rest or in uniform rectilinear motion as long as the resultant of the forces acting on it is zero. Inertia is the property of bodies to maintain their state of motion. Without external forces, a body does not change its velocity.

formulas.title: Law II
formulas.explanation: The resultant force acting on a body is equal to the product of mass and acceleration. Mass (m) measures the body's inertia: the greater the mass, the less the acceleration for the same force. Units: F in N (newton), m in kg, a in m/s².

formulas.title: The third law
formulas.explanation: Law of action and reaction: If body 1 acts on body 2 with force F₁₂, then body 2 acts on body 1 with force F₂₁ = −F₁₂. The forces have the same mode, the same direction, but opposite directions. It acts on different bodies.

formulas.title: The weight
formulas.explanation: Gravity is the force with which the Earth attracts a body. g is the gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface (varies slightly with latitude and altitude). Unit: N (newton). Example: a 10 kg body has a weight of G = 10·9.8 = 98 N.

formulas.title: Normal force
formulas.explanation: The normal force is the reaction of the supporting surface, perpendicular to the surface. On a plane inclined at angle θ, N = mg·cos θ. It balances the perpendicular component of weight. On the horizontal plane: N = mg.

formulas.title: Frictional force
formulas.explanation: The sliding friction force is proportional to the normal force. μ is the coefficient of friction (dimensionless, depends on the nature of the surfaces). Ff opposes the motion. In static friction: Ff ≤ μ·N (up to the maximum value that allows movement).

formulas.title: Force on inclined plane
formulas.explanation: The component of weight parallel to the inclined plane that causes the body to slide. The larger the angle θ, the larger F∥. At θ = 90° (free fall): F∥ = mg. This force is responsible for the acceleration of the body on the plane.

formulas.title: Mechanical work
formulas.explanation: Mechanical work is done by a force when its point of application moves. θ is the angle between the force and the direction of displacement. L = F·d when the force is parallel to the displacement. L > 0 (motive force), L < 0 (resistive force), L = 0 (perpendicular force). Unit: J (Jul).

formulas.title: Kinetic energy
formulas.explanation: Kinetic energy is the energy due to motion. It depends on the mass and the square of the velocity. Unit: J. A body at rest has Ec = 0. When the velocity is doubled, the kinetic energy increases by a factor of 4. It is a positive scalar quantity.

formulas.title: Theorem of mechanical work
formulas.explanation: The mechanical work of the resultant forces is equal to the change in kinetic energy. If L > 0, the body accelerates; if L < 0, the body brakes. This theorem is a form of the kinetic energy theorem and applies to any mechanical situation.

formulas.title: Gravitational potential energy
formulas.explanation: Gravitational potential energy depends on the height h above a reference level (usually the ground). Increases with h. When falling, Ep becomes Eq. The reference level is arbitrary; only ΔEp matters. Unit: J.

formulas.title: Conservation of mechanical energy
formulas.explanation: In the absence of non-conservative forces (friction, resistance), total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) is conserved. Energy can go from Ec to Ep and vice versa, but the amount remains constant. Example: pendulum, free fall without friction.

formulas.title: The power
formulas.explanation: Power measures the speed with which mechanical work is done. P = L/t (work per unit time). The form P = F·v is useful when force and velocity are constant and parallel. Unit: W (watt) = J/s. 1 HP ≈ 735 W.

formulas.title: return
formulas.explanation: Yield is the ratio of useful work (Lu) to consumed work (Lc). η ≤ 1 always; the difference is lost through friction, heat, etc. η = 1 only in ideal, lossless systems. It is often expressed as a percentage: η = 80% means η = 0.8.

mecanica.section: 5. Impulse and the amount of motion

formulas.title: The amount of movement
formulas.explanation: The quantity of motion (mechanical impulse) is a vector having direction and sense of velocity. It measures "inertia in motion". Unit: kg·m/s. In collisions, p total is conserved. A truck has higher p than a car at the same speed due to mass.

formulas.title: Momentum–momentum theorem
formulas.explanation: The impulse of the force (F·Δt) is equal to the change in momentum. For a constant force: F·Δt = m·Δv. In collisions, the forces are large and Δt small, so F can be very large. Explain why airbags increase Δt and decrease F.

formulas.title: Conservation of momentum
formulas.explanation: In an isolated system (resultant of external forces = 0), the total momentum is conserved. In collisions, the sum m·v before is equal to the sum m·v after. v' are the velocities after the collision. The equation is vector; applies to each axis.

formulas.title: Period
formulas.explanation: The period is the time it takes the body to complete one complete rotation (2π radians). Unit: s (second). T = 1/f, where f is the frequency. Example: the minutes of the clock have T = 60 s, so ω = 2π/60 rad/s.

formulas.title: Frequency
formulas.explanation: Frequency is the number of complete revolutions per second. Unit: Hz (hertz) = s⁻¹. f = ω/(2π). Example: a disk making 33 rotations/minute has f = 33/60 ≈ 0.55 Hz.

formulas.title: Angular velocity
formulas.explanation: Angular velocity measures the speed of rotation in radians per second. ω = 2π/T = 2πf. In MCU, ω is constant. Unit: rad/s. The connection with the period: the higher T is, the smaller ω is.

formulas.title: Linear speed
formulas.explanation: The linear (tangential) velocity is perpendicular to the radius. v = ω·r relates the angular velocity to the radius of the trajectory. Points farther from the center have larger v. v = 2πr/T = 2πrf. The direction changes continuously, but the module remains constant.

formulas.title: Centripetal acceleration
formulas.explanation: Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the center of the circle and only changes the direction of the velocity, not the magnitude. ac = v²/r = ω²r. In the MCU there is only centripetal acceleration, not tangential. Without the needle, the body would move in a straight line.

formulas.title: Centripetal force
formulas.explanation: Centripetal force is the resultant of the forces that keep the body on a circular path. Fc = m·ac. Examples: tension in the wire (tapered pendulum), friction (car turning), gravity (satellite in orbit). It is directed towards the center.

formulas.title: Newton's law
formulas.explanation: Two bodies attract with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between the centers. G is the universal gravitational constant. The law applies to point or spherical bodies. It explains both the fall of bodies and the motion of the planets.

formulas.title: Gravitational acceleration
formulas.explanation: Gravitational acceleration at the surface of a celestial body of mass M and radius R. At Earth: g ≈ 9.8 m/s². Decreases with altitude. On the Moon, g is ~6 times smaller. Allows calculation of g on other planets knowing M and R.

formulas.title: Orbital velocity
formulas.explanation: The speed a satellite must have to orbit at a distance r from the center of the planet (mass M). It results from equating the gravitational force with the centripetal force. The higher the orbit, the smaller v is. For ISS: v ≈ 7.7 km/s.

formulas.title: Kepler's third law
formulas.explanation: The square of the period of revolution is proportional to the cube of the semimajor axis of the orbit. Valid for all planets orbiting the same body (eg Sun). It allows the calculation of planetary distances or the mass of the Sun.

formulas.title: Moment of force
formulas.explanation: Moment of force (torque) measures the force's ability to produce rotation. d is the arm of the force (the distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force). Unit: N·m. M = 0 when the force passes through the axis. M = F·d·sin θ in general.

formulas.title: Equilibrium condition (translation)
formulas.explanation: For translational equilibrium, the resultant of the forces must be zero. The body does not translate. The first equilibrium condition for a rigid body.

formulas.title: Balance condition (rotation)
formulas.explanation: For rotational balance, the sum of the moments of the forces about any axis must be zero. The body does not rotate. The second equilibrium condition. The two conditions must be met simultaneously for complete equilibrium.

formulas.title: The fundamental law of rotation
formulas.explanation: The analog of F = ma for rotation: the resultant moment is equal to the product of the moment of inertia (I) and the angular acceleration (α). It depends on the shape of the body and the axis of rotation. Unit for I: kg·m².

formulas.title: Kinetic moment
formulas.explanation: Kinetic momentum (momentum of momentum) is the momentum analog for rotation. L = I·ω. It is conserved in isolated systems (eg the skater who squeezes his arms spins faster). Unit: kg·m²/s.

formulas.title: Rotational kinetic energy
formulas.explanation: The kinetic energy of a rotating body. Analogous to Ec = ½mv² for translation. A body can have both translational and rotational kinetic energy (eg the spinning wheel).

formulas.title: Hooke's law
formulas.explanation: The elastic force is proportional to the strain x and directed towards the equilibrium position (minus sign). k is the elastic constant of the spring (N/m). The stiffer the spring, the higher k is. Strength is restorative.

formulas.title: Elastic potential energy
formulas.explanation: Energy stored in a compressed or stretched spring with strain x. It is maximum at amplitude (x = ±A), zero at equilibrium. It is converted to kinetic energy and vice versa during oscillation. Similar form to Ec = ½mv².

formulas.title: Equation of motion
formulas.explanation: The law of motion of the harmonic oscillator. A = amplitude, ω = pulsation, φ = initial phase. The body oscillates between -A and +A. The cosine describes the periodic motion. v = dx/dt = -Aω·sin(ωt + φ).

formulas.title: The period of the elastic oscillator
formulas.explanation: The period of the oscillator (spring–mass) depends only on m and k, not on the amplitude (within the validity of Hooke's law). The bigger the mass or the smaller k, the bigger T is. ω = √(k/m).

formulas.title: The period of the simple pendulum
formulas.explanation: The period of the gravitational pendulum depends on the length of the string (l) and g. It does not depend on the mass of the pendulum. Valid for small oscillations (θ < ~10°). The longer pendulum swings slower. Useful for measuring g.

formulas.title: Maximum speed
formulas.explanation: The maximum speed is reached when passing through the equilibrium position (x = 0), where all the energy is kinetic. vmax = Aω. It depends on the amplitude and pulsation. At the elastic oscillator: vmax = A√(k/m).

formulas.title: The force of love
formulas.explanation: Air resistance (drag) is proportional to the square of the velocity, the cross-sectional area (A), the fluid density (ρ) and the drag coefficient (C_d). C_d depends on body shape: ~0.47 for a sphere, ~1.0–1.3 for a flat surface. Formula valid in turbulent regime (Re > ~1000).

formulas.title: Equation of falling motion with resistance
formulas.explanation: When falling through air, the body is subject to gravity (mg, down) and drag (up, opposite to motion). The acceleration decreases as the speed increases, until the drag balances the weight and a = 0.

formulas.title: Terminal velocity
formulas.explanation: Terminal velocity is the maximum velocity reached in the fall, when the drag force equals the weight (a = 0). It depends on mass, shape and area. Example: a skydiver achieves ~55 m/s with arms outstretched, ~90 m/s in aerodynamic position. A stretched sheet of paper has much lower v_t than the same crumpled sheet.

formulas.title: Velocity as a function of time (fall)
formulas.explanation: At small times, tanh ≈ gt/v_t, so v ≈ gt (free fall). At high times, tanh → 1, so v → v_t (terminal velocity). The transition is gradual; the body reaches ~99% of v_t after a time t ≈ 5 v_t/g.

formulas.title: Position over time (fall)
formulas.explanation: Distance traveled in resisted fall. At small times: y ≈ ½gt² (free fall). At large times: y ≈ v_t·t (uniform motion with terminal velocity). The graph of y(t) starts out parabolic and becomes linear.

formulas.title: Reynolds number
formulas.explanation: The Reynolds number (dimensionless) indicates the flow regime: Re < ~2000 → laminar (drag ∝ v), Re > ~4000 → turbulent (drag ∝ v²). ρ = fluid density, v = velocity, L = characteristic body length, μ = dynamic viscosity. In most practical cases (balls, parachutes, vehicles), Re is large and the v² formula is used.

formulas.title: Temperature conversion
formulas.explanation: To convert from Celsius to Kelvin, add 273. Example: 25°C = 298 K. In physics we use Kelvin because 0 K = the lowest possible temperature.

formulas.title: Linear expansion
formulas.explanation: When a body heats up, they elongate. α says how much (he's in trouble). l₀ = initial length, Δt = how much it heated up. Example: railroad tracks widen in summer.

formulas.title: Volume expansion
formulas.explanation: Same as linear dilation, but for volume. γ is approximately 3 times α. Liquids expand more than solids.

formulas.title: Atomic number
formulas.explanation: Z is the number of protons in the nucleus (and, in neutral atoms, the number of electrons). You can find it directly in the periodic table.

formulas.title: Mass number
formulas.explanation: A is the sum of protons (Z) and neutrons (N). In many problems, N lies with N = A − Z (using the given isotope).

formulas.title: The number of neutrons
formulas.explanation: If you know the isotope (A) and the atomic number (Z), you quickly find the number of neutrons in the nucleus.

formulas.title: Moths from the table
formulas.explanation: The molar mass M is taken from the periodic table (g/mol). The formula is essential when you go from mass to moles (eg: gases, mixtures).

formulas.title: Table of moths
formulas.explanation: Inverse of the formula above: if you know the moles, you get the mass of the substance.

formulas.title: The number of particles
formulas.explanation: Relate moles to number of particles (atoms/molecules). It appears often in ideal gas and atomic structure problems.

formulas.title: Avogadro's constant
formulas.explanation: The number of particles in a mol. Use it to switch between microscopic and macroscopic scales.

formulas.title: Molar concentration
formulas.explanation: Concentration (mol/L or mol/m³) occurs when working with solutions or distributions of particles in a volume V.

termodinamica.section: 2. The ideal gas — The gas laws

formulas.title: The equation of state
formulas.explanation: The master equation for an ideal gas. ν = number of moles. With it you calculate p, V or T when you know the others. R is a constant, you use it directly.

formulas.title: The general relationship for two states
formulas.explanation: If you know p, V and T in one state, you can calculate any quantity in the other state. All temperatures in Kelvin!

formulas.title: Isotherm (constant T): p and V
formulas.formula: \( p \cdot V = const. \) → \( p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2 \)
formulas.explanation: When the temperature remains constant: if you compress the gas (V decreases), the pressure increases. And vice versa. Example: syringe with closed cap.

formulas.title: Isobar (constant p): V and T
formulas.explanation: When the pressure remains constant: the gas expands on heating. The warmer it is, the more space it takes up. T must be in Kelvin!

formulas.title: Isochor (constant V): p and T
formulas.explanation: When the volume remains constant: on heating, the pressure increases. Example: gas cylinder or car tire in the sun.

formulas.title: The law of conservation of energy
formulas.explanation: Internal energy changes when the gas receives or gives up heat (Q) and when it does or receives mechanical work (L). Q > 0 = receives heat, L > 0 = is compressed (receives work).

formulas.title: Internal energy
formulas.explanation: The internal energy of the gas depends only on the temperature. Cv is a constant that depends on the type of gas (it is given in the problems).

formulas.title: Variation of internal energy
formulas.explanation: How much has the internal energy changed? It only depends on how much the temperature has changed, not the distance traveled. Use in any process.

formulas.title: Isochor — Mechanical work
formulas.explanation: At constant volume the gas does no work (nothing moves). All the heat received causes the temperature to rise.

formulas.title: Isochor — Heat and energy
formulas.explanation: In isochore, heat = change in internal energy (because L = 0). The more heat it receives, the more U increases.

formulas.title: Isobar — Mechanical work
formulas.explanation: At constant pressure, the gas can do work as it expands. Some of the heat becomes work, the rest increases the temperature.

formulas.title: Isobar — Heat
formulas.explanation: Heat at constant pressure. Cp is slightly greater than Cv (Cp = Cv + R). It is given in the tables.

formulas.title: Isothermal — Mechanical work
formulas.explanation: The work when the gas expands or compresses at constant T. ln = natural logarithm. In compression (V₂ < V₁) the work is negative.

formulas.title: Isotherm — Energy and Heat
formulas.explanation: At constant temperature the internal energy does not change. All the heat received is converted into work (or vice versa in compression).

formulas.title: Adiabatic — Energy
formulas.explanation: Adiabatic = no heat exchange with the outside. Anything done by gas comes from its internal energy. In adiabatic compression, the gas heats up!

formulas.title: Adiabatic — p–V relation
formulas.explanation: In adiabatic, p and V are related by this formula. γ ≈ 1.4 for air. You use it when you know p and V in one state and want to find out in another.

formulas.title: Heat engine efficiency
formulas.explanation: Efficiency = how much of the heat received (Q₁) was transformed into useful work (L). Q₂ = heat lost. The yield is always below 1 (below 100%).

formulas.title: Maximum yield (Carnot)
formulas.explanation: The maximum possible efficiency between a hot (T₁) and a cold (T₂) source. No real engine can be more efficient. Temperatures in Kelvin!

formulas.title: Entropy change
formulas.explanation: Entropy measures "disorder". When you get heat, entropy increases. T must be in Kelvin. It is used in Principle II.

formulas.title: Heat in heating/cooling
formulas.explanation: How much heat is needed to heat a mass m by ΔT degrees? c = specific heat (given: water has c ≈ 4200 J/(kg·K)).

formulas.title: Thermal balance
formulas.explanation: When you put a hot body in contact with a cold body, the heat given off by the hot body = the heat received by the cold body. Until equilibrium, when they have the same temperature.

formulas.title: Heat to change of state
formulas.explanation: When melting, vaporizing, etc. the temperature remains constant, but heat is needed. L = latent heat (of melting or vaporization), given in the tables.

formulas.title: Thermal conduction
formulas.explanation: How much heat passes through the wall in one second? λ = conductivity of the material (metal conducts well, wood poorly), A = area, d = thickness.

formulas.title: Thermal radiation
formulas.explanation: The power radiated by a body (without contact). Warm bodies radiate heat. The warmer it is, the more it radiates (T to the power of 4).

formulas.title: Cryogenic definition (usual threshold)
formulas.explanation: In engineering practice, cryogenics covers very low temperatures (of the order of tens-hundreds of kelvins). In this area the thermal and transport properties change strongly.

formulas.title: Ideal gas equation (basic model)
formulas.explanation: For the same number of particles n, decreasing the temperature T tends to decrease the pressure p if the volume remains fixed. In the simulator you see directly the connection between T, V and effective pressure.

formulas.title: Average molecular kinetic energy
formulas.explanation: Temperature directly controls the average energy of the particles. At lower T, the particles move more slowly, which favors condensation and local ordering.

formulas.title: Root Mean Square (RMS) Velocity
formulas.explanation: It shows the dependence of the velocity on temperature and molecular mass m. In the cryogenic regime, decreasing T strongly reduces the RMS velocity.

formulas.title: Stationary thermal conduction (1D)
formulas.explanation: Heat flow through cryogenic walls/insulations depends on conductivity k, area A, thickness L and thermal gradient. The formula explains why good insulation is critical in cryogenic vessels.

formulas.title: Simple cooling model (Newton's law)
formulas.explanation: It describes the temperature relaxation towards the ambient with a time constant \(\tau\). It is useful for quick estimates of cooling/heating time.

formulas.title: P wave velocity
formulas.explanation: The P wave (primary) is longitudinal; propagates through soil and fluids. It depends on the compressibility modulus K, the shear modulus G and the density ρ. Usually v_P > v_S.

formulas.title: The speed of the S wave
formulas.explanation: The S (secondary) wave is transverse — the particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation. It does not cross the ideal fluid. v_S depends on honey stiffness (G) and density.

formulas.title: Richter magnitude (local)
formulas.explanation: Logarithmic scale based on the amplitude of the wave recorded at a seismograph, relative to a reference amplitude A₀ (depends on distance and instrument). It is no longer the only scale used in practice.

formulas.title: Moment magnitude (moment scale)
formulas.explanation: Mw relates to the seismic moment M₀ (in N·m). It is more stable for large earthquakes than amplitude-only magnitudes.

formulas.title: The seismic moment
formulas.explanation: μ is the stiffness of the medium on the failure surface A, D is the mean slip. M₀ measures “how much” energy has been released by moving over a surface.

formulas.title: Seismic energy (empirical formula)
formulas.explanation: Indicative relationship between magnitude and released energy (in J, in forms usually cited in the literature). It is approximate: the actual energy depends on the fracture geometry and the environment.

formulas.title: The fundamental relationship
formulas.explanation: The phase velocity is the product of the wavelength λ and the frequency f. It relates the spatial and temporal parameters of the wave.

formulas.title: String speed
formulas.explanation: On an ideal string, v increases with tension T and decreases with linear mass μ (kg/m). Explain why the stretched or thinner string sounds sharper.

formulas.title: Progressive sine wave
formulas.explanation: Displacement at position x and time t for a propagating wave. k is the wave number, ω the pulse; φ is the initial phase. The sign in the argument decides the meaning of the propagation.

formulas.title: Wave number
formulas.explanation: The relation between λ and k: 2π radians of spatial phase fit into a space of one wavelength.

formulas.title: Wave energy on string (model)
formulas.explanation: Total energy proportional to square of amplitude and pulsation in a simple model (wave on string). The more vigorous the oscillation, the greater the energy.

formulas.title: The intensity of the wave
formulas.explanation: Average power per unit area. The second form (wave in medium) relates I to density ρ, velocity v, wave amplitude, and ω. Intensity decreases away from the source (geometry + absorption).

formulas.title: Snell's law
formulas.explanation: When passing between media, the product n·sin θ remains constant on the interface (incidence). Angles are measured relative to the normal.

formulas.title: The angle of deviation in the prism
formulas.explanation: δ is the angle by which the emerging beam is deviated from the incident one; A is the angle of the prism; θ₂′ is the angle of emergence on the second face.

formulas.title: Spectral refractive index
formulas.explanation: n depends on wavelength — the reason the prism breaks up white light (dispersion). Purple and red have different indices.

formulas.title: Cauchy's formula (dispersion)
formulas.explanation: Empirical model for n(λ) in visible; A, B, C match measurements. small λ (purple) → larger n, in general.

formulas.title: Minimum deviation
formulas.explanation: In the symmetrical configuration of the prism the minimum deviation occurs; useful relationship to experimentally determine n of the material.

formulas.title: Dispersing power (Abbe)
formulas.explanation: Measure of how far the colors are separated (Fraunhofer lines F, D, C). Materials with high P disperse more strongly.

formulas.title: Law of Motion (Harmonic)
formulas.explanation: Periodic motion with amplitude A, pulsation ω and initial phase φ. Extreme values ​​±A.

formulas.title: Speed
formulas.explanation: Derivative of displacement; the speed is maximum when passing through equilibrium (sin=0, cos=±1).

formulas.title: Acceleration
formulas.explanation: Acceleration is the opposite of displacement (restoration to the center) — the minus sign characterizes the harmonic oscillator.

formulas.title: The period of the gravitational pendulum
formulas.explanation: For small angles; depends on length l and g. Does not depend on mass (in the ideal model). The period increases by √l.

formulas.title: Damped pendulum equation
formulas.explanation: The term b dx/dt models the viscous friction; energy dissipates, amplitude decreases over time.

formulas.title: Damping coefficient
formulas.explanation: Parameter that quantifies how quickly the system loses energy relative to its undamped self-oscillation.

formulas.title: Damped pulsation
formulas.explanation: If γ < ω₀, the system oscillates with frequency slightly less than ω₀. If γ ≥ ω₀, the motion becomes aperiodic (critical or overdamped).

formulas.title: Logarithmic decrement
formulas.explanation: The consecutive ratio of the amplitudes on two oscillations; related to the energy loss per cycle. T_d is the amortized period.

formulas.title: Quality factor Q
formulas.explanation: High Q oscillator is hard to lose energy (narrow resonance in applications). Small Q → strong damping.

formulas.title: Non-linear pendulum (with correct model)
formulas.explanation: Exact form: restoring force ∝ sin φ, not φ. At large angles the period depends on the amplitude.

formulas.title: Period for big swings
formulas.explanation: K is the complete elliptic integral; depends on the amplitude. Generalize the small formula T = 2π√(l/g).

formulas.title: x(t) component
formulas.explanation: Harmonic oscillation on the x-axis; amplitude A₁, frequency ω₁, phase φ₁.

formulas.title: y(t) component
formulas.explanation: Independent oscillation on the y-axis. The trajectory (x, y) is the Lissajous curve.

formulas.title: Frequency ratio
formulas.explanation: If r is rational (eg 2/3), the figure is closed and periodic. Simple ratios give recognizable shapes.

formulas.title: Phase difference
formulas.explanation: Controls the shape and orientation of the figure when the frequency ratio is fixed (eg 1:1 gives ellipses or straight lines when Δφ = 0 or π/2).

formulas.title: Default relationship (r = 1)
formulas.explanation: Eliminating the time when ω₁ = ω₂, you get the peak traced conic; for different phases an ellipse generally appears.

formulas.title: Figure period
formulas.explanation: The time after which the trajectory repeats exactly, when the pulsations are commensurable (interpretation with the smallest multiple of the periods).

formulas.title: Energy (ideal 2D oscillator)
formulas.explanation: The sum of the maximum kinetic energies in the two directions in a simple model with the same mass m (order of magnitude).

formulas.title: Area (case r = 1)
formulas.explanation: The area of ​​the Lissajous ellipse when the frequencies are equal; becomes zero when the phases are aligned (movement in a straight line).

formulas.title: Current intensity
formulas.explanation: How much electric charge passes through a conductor in one second. I = current in Amps (A), Q in Coulombs (C), t in seconds. Example: 100 W bulb at 220 V has I ≈ 0.45 A.

formulas.title: The charge of the electron
formulas.explanation: Elemental charge — the smallest free charge in nature. All charges are multiples of e. The electron has −e, the proton +e. You use it in electron number problems.

formulas.title: Ohm's law
formulas.explanation: Voltage = resistance × current. Are you looking for U? Multiply R by I. Looking for I? Divide U by R. E is fundamental in any circuit.

formulas.title: Resistance of a conductor
formulas.explanation: The resistance depends on the material (ρ = resistivity), length (l) and section (A). Longer wire = more resistance. Thicker wire = less resistance. ρ is given in the tables.

formulas.title: Resistance with temperature
formulas.explanation: In metals, resistance increases with heating. R₀ = resistance at reference temperature, α = temperature coefficient (given). On coal, resistance decreases!

formulas.title: Series — Equivalent resistance
formulas.explanation: Resistors in series add up. Total resistance is greater than any. The current is the same through everything.

formulas.title: Series — Current and Voltage
formulas.explanation: In series, the current is the same everywhere. The source voltage is divided between the resistors: U = U₁ + U₂ + U₃.

formulas.title: Parallel — Equivalent resistance
formulas.explanation: In parallel, inverse of total resistance = sum of inverses. Total resistance is lower than any!

formulas.title: Parallel — Current and voltage
formulas.explanation: In parallel, the tension is the same in all. The total current is divided into branches: I = I₁ + I₂ + I₃.

formulas.title: Electric power
formulas.explanation: Power consumed by a receiver. P = U·I is the general form. When you only know R and I, you use R·I². When you know U and R, you use U²/R. Unit: Watt (W).

formulas.title: Electrical energy consumed
formulas.formula: \( W = P \cdot t = U \cdot I \cdot t \)
formulas.explanation: Energy = power × time. How much does a light bulb use in 2 hours? W = P·t. Unit: Joule (J) or kWh (1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J).

formulas.title: Joule effect (dissipated heat)
formulas.explanation: The heat given off by a resistor (ex: heater, light bulb). The higher the current, the more it heats up. Same as W, but in the form of heat.

formulas.title: Electromotive voltage
formulas.explanation: The source voltage (ε) is divided: one part on the circuit (U = terminal voltage), one part on the internal resistance (u).

formulas.title: Internal voltage drop
formulas.explanation: r = internal resistance of the source. When the current is high, u increases and U at the terminals decreases. The battery discharges when it supplies current.

formulas.title: Terminal voltage
formulas.explanation: The actual voltage that the circuit receives. It is less than ε when it is current. At idle (I = 0): U = ε.

formulas.title: Short circuit current
formulas.explanation: When the terminals are connected directly (without external resistance). Very high current! Dangerous — don't do this in practice.

formulas.title: Total and useful power
formulas.formula: \( P_{total} = \varepsilon \cdot I \) și \( P_{utila} = U \cdot I \)
formulas.explanation: Total power = what the source gives. Useful power = what the circuit receives. The difference is lost in the internal resistance.

formulas.title: Source yield
formulas.explanation: How much of the power of the source actually reaches the circuit. η = 1 (100%) when r = 0. In real batteries, η < 1.

formulas.title: Law I (knots)
formulas.explanation: In a node, current in = current out. What goes in, comes out. No current is lost in the node.

formulas.title: Second Law (eyes)
formulas.explanation: On a closed loop: sum of source voltages = sum of voltage drops across resistors. Pay attention to the signs (source and current)!

formulas.title: Electrical capacity
formulas.explanation: How much charge can the capacitor store at a given voltage. Big C = lots of charge. 1 F = 1 C/V.

formulas.title: Capacitance of the planar capacitor
formulas.explanation: C depends on the area of ​​the reinforcements (A), the distance between them (d) and the dielectric (εr). Bigger plate, closer together = higher C.

formulas.title: Stored energy
formulas.explanation: The energy in the charged capacitor. It is used for discharge (flash, defibrillator).

formulas.title: Capacitors in series
formulas.explanation: In series, the equivalent capacitance is less than either. As the inverse of resistors in parallel.

formulas.title: Capacitors in parallel
formulas.explanation: At the same time, capabilities are added. The total capacity increases.

formulas.title: Coulomb force
formulas.explanation: The force between two point charges. Charges of the same sign repel, opposite signs attract. r = distance between them.

formulas.title: The intensity of the electric field
formulas.explanation: The field created by a charge Q. E tells how much force there is per unit charge. Unit: N/C or V/m.

formulas.title: Uniform voltage and field
formulas.explanation: In a uniform field (eg between two parallel plates), voltage = field × distance. d = distance between points.

formulas.title: Electric potential energy
formulas.explanation: The energy of a charge q at the point where the voltage is U. When it moves, Ep is converted to kinetic energy or vice versa.

formulas.title: The effective value of the voltage
formulas.explanation: Effective voltage is the one that produces the same effect as direct current. At 220 V effective, U_max ≈ 311 V.

formulas.title: The effective value of the current
formulas.explanation: As with voltage. In the socket we have 220 V effective, 50 Hz. Current and voltage vary sinusoidally.

formulas.title: Instantaneous voltage
formulas.explanation: The typical model for a sinusoidal alternating voltage. U_max is the amplitude and ω = 2πf is the ripple.

formulas.title: Instantaneous current (phase shift)
formulas.explanation: In coil/capacitor circuits, the current can be out of phase by φ with respect to the voltage (they are not in phase).

formulas.title: The pulsation
formulas.explanation: Relates frequency (Hz) to pulsation (rad/s). In Romania, f = 50 Hz ⇒ ω ≈ 314 rad/s.

formulas.title: Alternating current power
formulas.explanation: cos φ = power factor. In pure resistor, cos φ = 1. In motors, cos φ < 1 ​​(there is reactive power).

formulas.title: Frequency in Romania
formulas.explanation: The voltage in the socket oscillates with 50 Hz. Period T = 1/f = 0.02 s. Once every 0.02 s the cycle is repeated.

formulas.title: Inductive reactance
formulas.explanation: The apparent resistance of the coil to alternating current. The higher the frequency, the higher the X_L. L = inductance (Henry).

formulas.title: Capacitive reactance
formulas.explanation: The apparent resistance of the capacitor to AC. The higher the frequency, the lower X_C. Opposite to the coil.

formulas.title: Impedance
formulas.explanation: The total resistance of the RLC circuit. Combine R, X_L and X_C. When X_L = X_C, Z = R (resonance).

formulas.title: Ohm's Law for AC
formulas.explanation: Same as DC but with Z instead of R. I and U are effective values.

formulas.title: Resonance frequency
formulas.explanation: At this frequency, X_L = X_C and Z = R (minimum). The circuit resonates, the current is maximum.

formulas.title: Superconducting phase condition
formulas.explanation: Below the critical temperature \(T_c\), the material enters the superconducting state and the magnetic response changes radically.

formulas.title: Effective resistivity in the superconducting state
formulas.explanation: In the ideal model, current can flow without significant Joule losses below \(T_c\).

formulas.title: Educational model of magnetic levitation
formulas.explanation: In the simulator, the repulsive force increases with \(B^2\) and decreases with the square of the distance from the superconducting surface.

formulas.title: Vertical balance
formulas.explanation: Law of vertical dynamics: Quasi-static levitation occurs when \(F_m\) offsets weight \(mg\).

formulas.title: London equation (compact form)
formulas.explanation: Basic relationship for magnetic field shielding in superconductors; underlies the interpretation of the Meissner effect.

formulas.title: Penetration depth London
formulas.explanation: The magnetic field penetrates the surface of the superconductor only for a characteristic distance \(\lambda_L\), then it is effectively shielded.

formulas.title: Global reaction
formulas.explanation: Hydrogen and oxygen react; chemical energy is partially converted into electrical energy by separating charges at the electrodes.

formulas.title: Electric power
formulas.explanation: The power delivered to the external circuit is the product of the terminal voltage and the load current.

formulas.title: Ohm's Law (load)
formulas.explanation: For a bulb modeled as a resistor \(R\), the current increases when the voltage increases or the resistance decreases (within the limits imposed by the reactance supply).

formulas.title: Indicative yield
formulas.explanation: Ratio between the useful electrical power and the power associated with the available chemical flow; H₂/O₂ imbalance or temperature affects efficiency in the model.

formulas.title: The law of reflection
formulas.formula: \( i = r \) (unghi de incidență = unghi de reflexie)
formulas.explanation: The incident and reflected rays make the same angle with the surface normal. Simple: as it goes in, so it comes out. The mirror reflects symmetrically.

formulas.title: The plane mirror
formulas.explanation: The image is at the same distance from the mirror as the object. If you stand 1 m from the mirror, your image is 1 m behind it. Virtual image, symmetrical.

formulas.title: The law of refraction
formulas.explanation: When light passes from one medium to another (ex: air to water), the ray is refracted. n₁, n₂ = refractive indices. The larger n, the smaller the angle.

formulas.title: Refractive index
formulas.explanation: n tells how many times slower light is in a medium than in a vacuum. Air: n ≈ 1. Water: n ≈ 1.33. Glass: n ≈ 1.5. The larger n, the slower the light.

formulas.title: Limit angle (total reflection)
formulas.explanation: When light comes from medium with higher n (ex: water) to one with lower n (air), there is an angle beyond which there is no more refraction, only reflection. Used for optical fibers.

formulas.title: The mirror equation
formulas.explanation: It relates focal length (f), object distance (d_o) and image distance (d_i). With the concave mirror you can get real or virtual images, depending on the position of the object.

formulas.title: Focal length
formulas.explanation: The focus is in the middle of the radius. Mirror with R = 20 cm has f = 10 cm. f > 0 = concave mirror, f < 0 = convex mirror.

formulas.title: Linear magnification
formulas.explanation: How big is the image relative to the object. negative m = inverted image. m positive = right image. |m| > 1 = enlarged image.

formulas.title: Sign conventions (mirrors)
formulas.formula: d_o > 0 obiect real; d_i > 0 imagine reală; d_i < 0 imagine virtuală; f > 0 concavă, f < 0 convexă
formulas.explanation: d_o always positive (the object is real). d_i > 0 when the image is in front of the mirror (concave), d_i < 0 when it is behind (virtual). Convex has negative f.

formulas.title: Lens Equation (Gauss)
formulas.explanation: Same as mirrors, but the conventions are different. f > 0 = converging (convex) lens, f < 0 = diverging (concave).

formulas.title: Vergence (optical power)
formulas.explanation: Lens power in diopters. 2 δ lens has f = 0.5 m = 50 cm. The higher the D, the stronger the lens.

formulas.title: Linear magnification
formulas.explanation: In lenses, m = d_i/d_o (no minus, unlike mirrors). m > 0 = upright image, m < 0 = inverted image.

formulas.title: Thin lens formula
formulas.explanation: The relationship between f, the index n of the glass and the radii of curvature R₁, R₂. Converging lens: R₁ and R₂ have matching signs.

formulas.title: Sign conventions (lenses)
formulas.formula: f > 0 convergentă; f < 0 divergentă; d_i > 0 imagine reală; d_i < 0 imagine virtuală
formulas.explanation: Real image = on the other side of the lens from the object (can be captured on the screen). Virtual image = same side, cannot be caught.

formulas.title: Contact lenses
formulas.explanation: Two lenses glued together have total vergence = sum of vergences. Two lenses of +2 δ and +3 δ give +5 δ.

optica.section: 5. The human eye and visual defects

formulas.title: The normal eye
formulas.formula: Vede clar între 10 cm (proxim) și infinit (remotum)
formulas.explanation: The healthy eye can focus from 10 cm to infinity. Below 10 cm we can no longer see clearly.

formulas.title: Myopia
formulas.explanation: Myopia sees well near, but not far. The focus is too close. Glasses with concave (divergent) lenses move the image away.

formulas.title: longsightedness
formulas.explanation: Hypermetropia sees well far, but not near. Glasses with convex (convergent) lenses bring the image closer.

formulas.title: The power of correction
formulas.explanation: For myopia: D negative, d_remotum = maximum distance at which he sees clearly (in m). For hypermetropia: D positive.

formulas.title: Microscope magnification
formulas.explanation: Total magnification = objective magnification × eyepiece magnification. The microscope has two lenses: the objective (closer to the object) and the eyepiece (closer to the eye).

formulas.title: Magnifying glass
formulas.explanation: 25 cm = conventional clear vision distance. Magnifying glass with f = 5 cm magnifies 5 times. The smaller f is, the higher the magnification.

formulas.title: Scope/telescope magnification
formulas.explanation: Magnification = focal ratio. The objective has a large f (captures a lot of light), the eyepiece has a small f. Good telescope: large f_ob, small f_oc.

formulas.title: The visible spectrum
formulas.formula: ROGVAIV (roșu, oranj, galben, verde, albastru, indigo, violet)
formulas.explanation: White light (sun) contains all colors. The prism breaks them down: each color has a different n and refracts differently.

formulas.title: The index depends on λ
formulas.explanation: n is larger for violet (small λ) and smaller for red (large λ). Violet refracts more, red less. Hence the rainbow.

formulas.title: Maxim (bright fringes)
formulas.explanation: When the path difference (Δ) is a multiple of λ, the waves strengthen = bright fringe. k = the order of the maximum.

formulas.title: Minimum (dark fringes)
formulas.explanation: When Δ is an odd multiple of λ/2, the waves cancel = dark fringe.

formulas.title: Distance between fringes (Young)
formulas.explanation: L = distance to screen, d = distance between the two slots. With larger λ or larger L, the fringes are further apart.

formulas.title: Minimum at single slot
formulas.explanation: a = slot width. Light scatters when it passes through a narrow slit. First minima at k = ±1.

formulas.title: Diffraction grating — max
formulas.explanation: The lattice has many parallel slits at distance d. The maxima are very sharp. Used in the spectroscope to separate colors.

formulas.title: Photon energy
formulas.explanation: Light is made up of photons. Each photon has energy h·f. With higher frequency (lower λ), the photon is more energetic.

formulas.title: Einstein's equation
formulas.formula: \( E_k = h \cdot f - L \) (L = lucrul de extracție)
formulas.explanation: The kinetic energy of the extracted electron = the energy of the photon minus the extraction work (minimum energy to remove the electron).

formulas.title: Photoelectric threshold
formulas.explanation: The minimum frequency for which the photoelectric effect occurs. Below f_min, even if the light is strong, no electrons come out. It's a problem of energy, not intensity.

formulas.title: The wave–frequency relationship
formulas.explanation: Relates wavelength and frequency. For light in a vacuum, c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s. The laser is almost monochromatic (λ well defined).

formulas.title: Photon energy
formulas.explanation: Photon energy increases as frequency increases (λ decreases). UV has more energetic photons than IR.

formulas.title: The momentum of the photon
formulas.explanation: Even light carries momentum; occurs in radiation pressure and laser optics (trapping) applications.

formulas.title: The intensity
formulas.explanation: The laser can focus the power on a small area, increasing the intensity (W/m²).

formulas.title: The inverse square law
formulas.explanation: Valid for sources that radiate approximately spherically. For collimated (laser) beams the decrease with r can be much slower.

formulas.title: Divergence (approx. Gaussian)
formulas.explanation: Diffraction limit: the narrower the beam (low w₀), the greater the divergence.

formulas.title: Rayleigh distance
formulas.explanation: Up to zR the beam remains relatively collimated; after that it starts to widen visibly.

formulas.title: The wave–frequency relationship
formulas.explanation: Same relationship for all electromagnetic waves (radio → gamma). It only changes f and λ.

formulas.title: Photon energy
formulas.explanation: X-ray and gamma photons have much higher energies than those in the visible.

formulas.title: The momentum of the photon
formulas.explanation: When λ decreases (f increases), the momentum of the photon increases.

formulas.title: Wien law
formulas.explanation: The maximum of the radiation spectrum of a body depends on the temperature. Higher T ⇒ lower λ_max (more “blue”).

formulas.title: Stefan–Boltzmann
formulas.explanation: The radiated power increases very quickly with temperature (T⁴). It explains why very hot bodies radiate intensely.

formulas.title: The inverse square law
formulas.explanation: The intensity decreases with the square of the distance for a point source (ex: ideal isotropic antenna).

formulas.title: The wave-frequency relationship
formulas.explanation: Relate wavelength and frequency for vacuum propagation. Dacă λ scade, frecvența crește, iar fotonii devin mai energetici.

formulas.title: Photon energy
formulas.explanation: A shorter wavelength laser carries more energetic photons. Formula este esențială când compari lasere IR, vizibile sau UV.

formulas.title: The momentum of the photon
formulas.explanation: Even though it has no rest mass, the photon carries momentum. This is where radiation pressure and momentum transfer effects into matter arise.

formulas.title: Beam intensity
formulas.explanation: For the same total power, a smaller spot area means higher intensity. This is why focus is so important in experiments.

formulas.title: The area of ​​the circular spot
formulas.explanation: Approximation for the spot area around the characteristic radius w₀. Decreasing w₀ rapidly increases the intensity.

formulas.title: Gaussian divergence
formulas.explanation: Beams that are very tight in focus tend to open up more quickly after focusing. The relation expresses the limit imposed by diffraction.

formulas.title: Rayleigh distance
formulas.explanation: Over a distance of the order of zR, the beam remains relatively well collimated around the focus. Beyond this area, the diameter increases noticeably.

formulas.title: Peak pulse power
formulas.explanation: If the same pulse energy is compressed into a very short time, the instantaneous power increases enormously. This is one of the key principles of ultrafast lasers.

formulas.title: Peak intensity
formulas.explanation: Combines peak power with spot area. High intensities are those that can produce ablation, plasma or advanced ionization.

formulas.title: Radiation pressure
formulas.explanation: Light exerts pressure by momentum transfer. For a perfectly reflective surface, the effect is roughly double that of absorption.

formulas.title: Energy density
formulas.explanation: It shows how much electromagnetic energy there is per unit volume in a propagating beam. The relation helps to interpret the extreme regimes.

formulas.title: Simplified model for the plasma wave
formulas.explanation: In the educational model, the laser pulse creates a plasma wave (wakefield). The amplitude A is related to the intensity, and the wave number k to the plasma density.

formulas.title: Spot focused intensity
formulas.explanation: With the same P laser power, a smaller spot gives a higher intensity. In the simulator, increasing the intensity leads to stronger acceleration fields.

formulas.title: The Lorentz factor
formulas.explanation: It shows the entry into the relativistic regime: when the electron speed v approaches c, the value of γ increases rapidly and the energy of the particle increases significantly.

formulas.title: The relativistic energy of the electron
formulas.explanation: The formula directly relates the energy of the electron to the Lorentz factor. When the electron remains synchronized with the accelerating phase of the wakefield, E increases more efficiently.

formulas.title: Linear function
formulas.explanation: Straight line with slope a and ordered at the origin b. Uniform growth model; a = Δy/Δx on any interval.

formulas.title: Quadratic function
formulas.explanation: Parable. His sign to tell whether the branches are up or down; peak at x = −b/(2a) (zero derivative).

formulas.title: Derivative (definition)
formulas.explanation: The slope of the tangent to the graph of f versus x—instantaneous rate of change. Fundamental to all derivation rules.

formulas.title: The derivative of the sine
formulas.explanation: Often used in oscillations and waves; the derivative of the cosine follows with changed sign.

formulas.title: Derivative of cosine
formulas.explanation: Couple with the sine; the minus sign reflects the π/2 phase shift between sin and cos.

formulas.title: The derivative of the exponential
formulas.explanation: e^x is its own derivative — which is why it appears in exponential growth and differential equations.

formulas.title: The derivative of the natural logarithm
formulas.explanation: Valid for x > 0. Bind relative increments: d(ln x) = dx/x.

formulas.title: Minkowski metric
formulas.explanation: The invariant interval in special relativity (signature +−−−). The "real" distance between events in spacetime does not depend on the inertial observer.

formulas.title: Right ascension and declination (notation)
formulas.explanation: Equatorial coordinates on the celestial sphere: α measured in hr/min/sec along the celestial equator, δ as angle to the equator (similar to latitude).

formulas.title: Angular distance on the celestial sphere
formulas.explanation: The angle θ between two directions to the stars in coordinates (α₁,δ₁) and (α₂,δ₂). Used for vault separations and observation conditions.

formulas.title: Apparent magnitude (Pogson)
formulas.explanation: Logarithmic scale: star with lower m appears brighter. Difference of 5 magnitudes ≈ factor 100 in flux.

formulas.title: Parallax distance (parsec)
formulas.explanation: The heliocentric parallax p (in seconds of arc) gives the distance in parsecs. The base is the radius of Earth's orbit (~1 AU).

formulas.title: Kepler's first law - the ellipse
formulas.explanation: The orbit is an ellipse; The sun in a focus. a = semi-major axis, e = eccentricity, b = semi-minor axis.

formulas.title: Kepler's second law - areas
formulas.explanation: The vector ray sweeps equal areas in equal times—the planet moves faster at perihelion, slower at aphelion.

formulas.title: Kepler's third law
formulas.explanation: The period T is related to the semimajor axis of a; for the same central body M, the ratio T²/a³ is the same for all satellites.

formulas.title: Average orbital velocity
formulas.explanation: The average length of the orbit (≈ 2πa for nearly circular orbit) divided by the period.

formulas.title: Elliptical orbit energy
formulas.explanation: The total energy of the low-mass system m in bound orbit is negative and depends only on the semimajor axis, not the eccentricity.

formulas.title: Velocity at perihelion
formulas.explanation: The maximum speed on the ellipse, at the minimum distance from the star (when the eccentricity e > 0).

formulas.title: Aphelion speed
formulas.explanation: The minimum speed on the ellipse, at the maximum distance from the star.

formulas.title: Universal gravity
formulas.explanation: The force between two point masses or spheres (their center). Newton's law of attraction at a distance.

formulas.title: Gravitational force (Newton)
formulas.explanation: In the planetary motion simulator, each planet is pulled toward the star with this force; gives the required centripetal acceleration of the orbit.

formulas.title: Velocity in circular orbit
formulas.explanation: Balance condition between gravity and circular motion: the larger r, the smaller v orbital.

formulas.title: Specific mechanical energy (elliptical orbit)
formulas.explanation: Energy per unit mass for bound orbit; directly related to the semimajor axis of (same idea as total E, but per mass).

formulas.title: Perihelion precession (general relativity, simplified idea)
formulas.explanation: The angle by which the axis of the ellipse rotates per revolution in RG — very small for most planets, measurable for Mercury; depends on M, a, e.

formulas.title: Parallel arm time (approx., v ≪ c)
formulas.explanation: In the model with aether and v small with respect to c, the round-trip time on the arm parallel to the "aether wind" contains a correction of order v²/c².

formulas.title: Perpendicular arm time (approx.)
formulas.explanation: On the perpendicular arm, the path in the ether system is slightly different, so the v²/c² order correction also differs from the parallel arm.

formulas.title: Expected time difference (ether model)
formulas.explanation: There would be phase shift in the interferometer if absolute ether existed; the experiment did not find the effect—supports the invariance of the speed of light.

formulas.title: Bohr level energy (hydrogen)
formulas.explanation: Quantified levels for the electron in Bohr's model: n = 1 is the ground (–13.6 eV); n → ∞ corresponds to ionization (0 eV).

formulas.title: Rydberg's formula
formulas.explanation: Wavelengths of emission/absorption spectra at H: m to n level transitions (m > n in emission). R_H ≈ 1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹.

formulas.title: Photon – energy and frequency
formulas.explanation: Light quantum: the energy related to the frequency of the electromagnetic wave; explain atomic spectra and the photoelectric effect.

formulas.title: De Broglie wavelength
formulas.explanation: Particles also have wave behavior; λ decreases as momentum p increases—used in electron diffraction.

formulas.title: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
formulas.explanation: You cannot simultaneously know position and momentum with arbitrary precision; fundamental limit in quantum mechanics.

atomul.section: Periodic table and amount of substance

formulas.title: Atomic number (Z) = number of protons
formulas.explanation: Z is the number of protons in the nucleus; in neutral atom coincides with the number of electrons. You read it directly from the periodic table.

formulas.title: Mass Number (A)
formulas.explanation: A sums up the protons and neutrons in the nucleus. The isotope is indicated by A along with the symbol of the element.

formulas.title: Number of neutrons (N)
formulas.explanation: With A and Z known, you quickly find out how many neutrons the nucleus has: N = A − Z.

formulas.title: The number of moles
formulas.explanation: The molar mass M (g/mol) is taken from the periodic table. The m/M ratio gives moles of substance — essential in gases and stoichiometry.

formulas.title: Mass of a substance (in moles)
formulas.explanation: Inverse of the previous formula: from the number of moles and the molar mass you get the mass in grams.

formulas.title: The number of particles
formulas.explanation: Relate moles to number of atoms or molecules: multiply by Avogadro's constant N_A.

formulas.title: Avogadro's constant
formulas.explanation: The number of elementary entities (atoms, molecules...) in a mole; used when switching between the macroscopic and microscopic scale.

formulas.title: Molar concentration
formulas.explanation: Molar concentration (mol/L or mol/m³) relates the number of moles to the volume of the solution or mixture.

formulas.title: Road difference and maxima
formulas.explanation: For two slits at distance d, the path difference to a point on the screen depends on the angle to the axis of symmetry. Intensity maxima occur when this difference is an integer multiple of the wavelength.

formulas.title: Spacing between fringes (Young, small angle)
formulas.explanation: On a screen at distance L from the slits, the approximate distance between two maxima uses the small angle approximation for sin and tang.

formulas.title: Superposition of amplitudes
formulas.explanation: In the linear quantum description, the amplitude before measurement is the sum of the contributions associated with the two paths. The relative phase decides whether the waves are strengthening or weakening.

formulas.title: Born's rule (probability)
formulas.explanation: The probability of detecting the particle in an area is proportional to the square of the modulus of the wave function in that area.

formulas.title: 1D stationary Schrödinger
formulas.explanation: The equation for states with energy E is well defined. In each region where the potential V is constant, the solution is a combination of real or complex exponentials, as the energy is greater or less than V.

formulas.title: Parameters k and κ (barrier, E below V₀)
formulas.explanation: k describes the spatial oscillation in the classically allowed zone; κ measures how fast the wave modulus decreases inside the barrier (classical forbidden region).

formulas.title: Transmission (typical behavior, thick barrier)
formulas.explanation: For a barrier of width a, the tunneling probability decreases exponentially with the product κ·a. The factors above depend on the exact model of the barrier.

formulas.title: The energy-time uncertainty principle
formulas.explanation: Finite lifetime states (eg tunneling from a meta-stable level) have a width in energy related to the characteristic time of the process.

fizicaCuantica.section: 3. Bonds between atoms and molecular orbitals

formulas.title: Combining atomic orbitals (bonding/antibonding MO)
formulas.explanation: Two atomic wave functions (eg two 1s orbitals) can combine linearly to give one bonding (symmetric) and one antibonding (antisymmetric) molecular orbital.

formulas.title: Binding energy
formulas.explanation: Binding energy is the energy required to separate the atoms of a molecule to infinity (state of free atoms).

formulas.title: Approximate bond strength (oscillator model)
formulas.explanation: Around the equilibrium distance r₀ between the nuclei, the bond potential can be approximated by a harmonic oscillator potential, with effective constant k.

formulas.title: Probability density in the link area
formulas.explanation: The probability of finding the electrons in the region between the nuclei is given by the square of the modulus of the bond wave function; a higher density between nuclei corresponds to covalent bonding.

formulas.title: The mole fraction of D₂O
formulas.explanation: Expresses the molar weight of heavy water in the mixture. In the simulator, the slider displays this percentage as an educational model.

formulas.title: Percent D₂O
formulas.explanation: Direct conversion of mole fraction to percent. The value is used in the simulator for the OK / Caution / High / Critical visual codes.

formulas.title: Indicative concentration
formulas.explanation: Useful relationship when you want to relate the amount of D₂O to the volume. No clinical calculation is done in the simulator, only a didactic representation of the composition.

formulas.title: Boiling point difference
formulas.explanation: At 1 atm, the simulator highlights the indicative values ​​100.0°C (H₂O) and 101.4°C (D₂O), so ΔTb is positive.

formulas.title: Freezing point difference
formulas.explanation: In the indicative data from the simulator, D₂O freezes higher (~3.8°C) than H₂O (~0°C), so ΔTf > 0.

formulas.title: Density ratio
formulas.explanation: The simulator uses guidance values ​​of ~1.00 g/cm³ for H₂O and ~1.11 g/cm³ for D₂O. It follows that the same volume of D₂O is heavier.

formulas.title: The ratio of vibrational frequencies
formulas.explanation: When the reduced mass increases (from H₂O to D₂O), the characteristic frequency decreases. This exact trend is illustrated in the slider experiment in the simulator.

formulas.title: Natural abundance of deuterium
formulas.explanation: In natural water, deuterium is a small fraction of the total hydrogen atoms. That is why ordinary water contains only traces of D₂O.

formulas.title: Simplified model of slowing down neutrons
formulas.explanation: The Reactor part uses a conceptual scheme: more collisions => lower neutron energy. In the model, D₂O retains more available neutrons than H₂O.

formulas.title: Separation factor
formulas.explanation: It measures the efficiency of isotopic separation between two phases (or two streams in equilibrium). In teaching simulators, increasing α accelerates deuterium enrichment.

formulas.title: Mass balance for deuterium
formulas.explanation: Deuterium conservation in a separation unit: what enters with the feed (F) is found in product (P) and residue (W).

formulas.title: Floor Enrichment (approx.)
formulas.explanation: Simplified model to illustrate the trend: more useful floors n and a better separation factor lead to higher D₂O concentrations.

formulas.title: Overall yield
formulas.explanation: It shows how much of the deuterium actually ends up in the product stream. In practice it depends on reflux, losses and the efficiency of the contact stages.

formulas.title: Induced fission (symbolic form)
formulas.explanation: The neutron is captured; the nucleus splits into two major fragments, emits ν neutrons and γ radiation. The concrete channels (masses, Z) vary; conserve mass number and charge.

formulas.title: Conservation of mass and load
formulas.explanation: In the model with two major fragments and ν neutrons, the sum of the mass numbers and the sum of the atomic numbers remain those of the reactants.

formulas.title: Cumulative energy (didactic benchmark in the simulator)
formulas.explanation: N is the number of fissions; the simulator uses ~200 MeV per event as the order of magnitude for the energy released (does not include reactor structure details).

formulas.title: Mass and Q defect
formulas.explanation: The energy released comes from the mass difference between the initial state and the products (including emitted neutrons), according to E = Δm·c².

formulas.title: Multiplying factor (simplified idea)
formulas.explanation: Ratio of useful neutrons from the next generation to those from the current generation. In the simulator, k is estimated empirically from fission rates, not from detailed criticality calculations.

formulas.title: Mass number and neutrons
formulas.explanation: A is the number of nucleons (protons + neutrons). For uranium, Z = 92; the isotope is identified by A (eg 235 for U-235).

formulas.title: α decay
formulas.explanation: The nucleus emits a cluster of two protons and two neutrons bound as helium-4; the son has Z 2 and A 4 less than the parent.

formulas.title: Decay constant
formulas.explanation: T₁/₂ is the time half of the nuclei of a type survive; τ (mean life) is related to λ by τ = 1/λ.

formulas.title: Decay Law (Number of Nuclei Remaining)
formulas.explanation: The Poisson process at the individual nucleus level gives an exponential decay of the macroscopic population N(t); same shape for each isotope, with different λ.

formulas.title: Form with halves
formulas.explanation: Equivalent to exp(-λt); useful when counting how many T₁/₂ periods have passed (in "time" teaching simulations).

formulas.title: Speed ​​of light (invariant in vacuum)
formulas.explanation: Exact value in SI from definition; all inertial observers measure the same c for light in a vacuum, regardless of the speed of the source.

formulas.title: Time dilation
formulas.explanation: The moving clock relative to the observer appears to run more slowly: the intervals Δt (at rest in the clock system) appear longer by a factor of γ in another system.

formulas.title: Length contraction
formulas.explanation: The length measured in the direction of motion is shortened by 1/γ compared to the length at rest (small effect up to speeds comparable to c).

formulas.title: Lorentz transformations (x, t)
formulas.explanation: It relates the space-time coordinates between two inertial references in relative motion with velocity v; replace Galilean transformations at high speeds.

formulas.title: The relativistic composition of velocities
formulas.explanation: The addition of speeds is no longer linear; the result never exceeds c, even though u and v are close to c.

formulas.title: Total relativistic energy
formulas.explanation: The total energy of the particle with rest mass m including the kinetic energy; for small v we find approximately Ec ≈ ½mv² + mc².

formulas.title: Resting energy
formulas.explanation: Energy equivalent to mass even at rest — the famous E = mc²: mass and energy are aspects of the same quantity.

formulas.title: Relativistic impulse
formulas.explanation: The generalization p = mv: the γ factor ensures conservation of momentum and energy in collisions at any speed.
